```{r setup, include=FALSE}
set.seed(486649)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center", fig.pos = "H", out.width = "78%",
  fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.6)
library(knitr); library(kableExtra)
find_data <- function(f) {
  cands <- c(file.path("../../processed_data", f),
             file.path("processed_data", f), f)
  hit <- cands[file.exists(cands)]
  if (!length(hit)) stop("Not found: ", f); hit[1]
}
fig <- function(f) { c(file.path("figure", f), f)[file.exists(c(file.path("figure", f), f))][1] }
m1  <- read.csv(find_data("tier1_metrics.csv"))
c1  <- read.csv(find_data("tier1_coefs.csv"))
a2  <- read.csv(find_data("tier2_auc_by_landmark.csv"))
gm  <- read.csv(find_data("tier3_gee.csv"))
cx  <- read.csv(find_data("tier3_tvcox.csv"))
ut  <- read.csv(find_data("tier4_utility.csv"))
al  <- read.csv(find_data("tier4_alarm_sweep.csv"))
sg  <- read.csv(find_data("tier5_subgroups.csv"))
gc  <- read.csv(find_data("tier6_mortality_cox.csv"))
go  <- read.csv(find_data("tier6_onset_assoc.csv"))
gm6 <- read.csv(find_data("tier6_gbtm_class_means.csv"))
ce  <- read.csv(find_data("tier7_effect_estimates.csv"))
en_auc <- m1$auroc[m1$model == "Tier1 full-feature elastic net"]
p1_auc <- m1$auroc[grepl("0.755", m1$model)]
alpha <- gm$OR_glm[gm$term == "__alpha_within_patient__"]
se_infl_max <- max(gm$SE_inflation, na.rm = TRUE)
best_u <- ut[which.max(ut$utility_norm), ]
op90 <- al[which.min(abs(al$sensitivity - 0.90)), ]
op50 <- al[which.min(abs(al$sensitivity - 0.50)), ]
K6 <- length(unique(gm6$class))
psm_row <- ce[ce$method == "PSM (1:1 nearest, ATT)", ]
ipw_row <- ce[ce$method == "IPW (ATE weights)", ]
aipw_row <- ce[ce$method == "AIPW / doubly robust (ATE)", ]
```

# Objective and what the earlier analysis established

This report is the second half of one research programme: predicting sepsis
onset *in real time* from MIMIC-IV ICU time series. The earlier stage
(scripts 01-09) built the temporal substrate: a 3.1M-row hourly panel, an
hourly Sepsis-3 onset label, and a leakage-safe hour-6 landmark cohort of
`r format(a2$n_at_risk[a2$landmark_h==6], big.mark=",")` at-risk stays, and
quantified the bar: a multivariable hourly logistic model reached a
cross-validated AUROC of about **`r sprintf("%.3f", p1_auc)`** for incident
onset within 12h, out-discriminating SOFA, qSOFA and SIRS. This report builds
the real-time model itself and closes two gaps the literature review
identified against comparable MIMIC-IV statistical studies: group-based
trajectory modelling (GBTM) and propensity-based confounder adjustment. Per
the project's design decision, all seven tiers below are built **entirely
from classical statistics**, no gradient boosting, no neural sequence
models, reaching real-time prediction through **dynamic landmarking** (van
Houwelingen 2007).

# Tier 1: the statistical ceiling (a full-feature nomogram at hour 6)

The earlier multivariable model deliberately handicapped itself to
non-circular predictors and, because plain complete-case regression cannot
use the 70-88%-missing labs at hour 6, effectively dropped them. Tier 1
removes both limits: an elastic-net penalized logistic model over the full
feature set, with the missing labs handled by an **informative-missingness
design** (median imputation plus a "was it measured" indicator per lab and
per trajectory slope). Evaluation is patient-grouped 5-fold CV with the
penalty strength chosen by an inner cross-validation on each training fold.

```{r t1tab}
m1d$delong_p_vs_baseline_traj <- ifelse(is.na(m1d$delong_p_vs_baseline_traj),
   "-", formatC(m1d$delong_p_vs_baseline_traj, format="e", digits=1))
kable(m1d, booktabs = TRUE, col.names = c("Model","AUROC","PR-AUC","Brier","DeLong p vs 0.755"),
      caption = "Discrimination at the hour-6 landmark (out-of-sample). The full-feature elastic net is the purely-statistical ceiling.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position","scale_down"))
```

The full-feature model reaches AUROC **`r sprintf("%.3f", en_auc)`**, a
statistically significant gain over the earlier `r sprintf("%.3f", p1_auc)`
model (DeLong *p* `r format.pval(m1$delong_p_vs_baseline_traj[nrow(m1)], digits=2, eps=1e-16)`),
with improved PR-AUC. The most striking finding is *what* carries the signal:
the largest coefficients are **missingness indicators**: whether a P/F ratio,
creatinine or WBC was drawn, and whether enough data existed to compute a
trajectory slope. The act of ordering a test encodes the clinician's evolving
suspicion, exactly the informative missingness the earlier report flagged but
could not exploit. Total SOFA enters with an *inverse* sign, consistent with
high organ dysfunction marking prevalent rather than incident disease.

```{r t1coef}
top <- c1[order(-abs(c1$coef)), ]; top <- top[top$term != "(Intercept)", ][1:10, ]
kable(top, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Feature","Coefficient","Odds ratio"),
      caption = "Ten largest standardized effects in the Tier-1 model (\\_msg = measurement indicator).") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

The result stops short of the 0.80-0.83 the README projected, and honestly so:
at a 6-hour landmark the labs that would lift discrimination are mostly not yet
drawn, so their imputed values add little beyond the fact of their absence.
`r sprintf("%d", nrow(c1)-1)` of the 27 candidate features survive penalization.

# Tier 2: the real-time deliverable (a dynamic landmark supermodel)

A single landmark answers "predict from hour 6". A deployed system must predict
at *every* hour. The classical solution is a **landmark supermodel**: repeat the
landmark construction on a grid of prediction hours *s* in {6,12,18,24,36,48},
stack them, and fit one penalized model with the landmark time *s*, $s^2$ and
feature-by-*s* interactions, so evaluating it at the current hour yields an
hourly-updating risk. Folds are grouped by patient (each stay recurs across
landmarks), and features remain only-past.

```{r t2tab}
kable(a2, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Landmark hour s","At risk","Onset in 12h","AUROC supermodel","AUROC separate"),
      caption = "Dynamic discrimination AUC(s): one supermodel evaluated at each prediction hour, versus fitting a separate model per landmark.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

```{r auc-s, fig.cap="AUC(s): the supermodel's out-of-sample discrimination as a function of the hour at which the prediction is made, versus per-landmark models.", out.width="62%"}
include_graphics(fig("auc_by_landmark.png"))
```

The single supermodel matches, at every prediction hour, the accuracy of
fitting a bespoke model per landmark while being one parsimonious,
deployable object. Discrimination is highest early (AUROC
`r sprintf("%.2f", a2$auc_supermodel[a2$landmark_h==6])` at hour 6), dips in the
mid-stay window (hours 18-24) where incident onset is rarest and hardest, and
recovers later. This *is* the real-time model, produced without leaving the
statistics domain.

# Tier 3: modelling the within-patient correlation

The earlier analysis never addressed that repeated hourly rows from one
patient are correlated. Two classical repeated-measures tools close that gap
on the sampled panel, using a proper dynamic outcome (incident onset within
12h, evaluated only on at-risk hours). A per-patient random-intercept GLMM is
*degenerate* for this outcome: most patients never have an event, so their
intercepts diverge. So we use the population-averaged route instead.

A **GEE** with an exchangeable working correlation estimates a within-patient
correlation of **`r sprintf("%.2f", alpha)`**: a patient's hourly observations
are strongly dependent, so the effective information is far below the
`r format(76538, big.mark=",")` row count. The consequence for inference is
concrete: putting **cluster-robust (sandwich) standard errors** on the pooled
logistic model, versus the naive model-based ones that assume independent hours,
inflates the SEs by up to **`r sprintf("%.1fx", se_infl_max)`**. A naive pooled
GLM would therefore report spuriously tight confidence intervals and
over-confident "significant" effects. A ridge-penalized **time-varying-covariate
Cox** model on the counting-process form gives directionally sensible
instantaneous hazards of onset:

```{r t3tab-gee}
gtab <- gm[gm$term != "__alpha_within_patient__", ]
kable(gtab, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Term","OR","SE naive","SE cluster-robust","SE inflation"),
      caption = "Pooled logistic model: naive vs cluster-robust (by patient) standard errors. Ignoring within-patient correlation understates every SE.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

```{r t3tab-cox}
cx$direction <- ifelse(cx$HR > 1, "raises hazard", "lowers hazard")
kable(cx, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Covariate (standardized)","Hazard ratio","Interpretation"),
      caption = "Ridge time-varying Cox: hazard of incident onset per SD of the evolving vital.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

These are inferential, correlation-correct companions to the predictive
supermodel, not competitors to it.

# Tier 4: real-time evaluation (utility and alarm burden)

Discrimination is necessary but not sufficient for a streaming alarm. Using the
supermodel to emit an hourly risk on a held-out 6,000-stay
set (trained on the rest, no leakage), we evaluate it as the field does. (The 6,000-stay holdout is scored at every
hour from hour 6 to onset or discharge.)

The **PhysioNet/CinC-2019 utility score**: which rewards early detection and
penalizes both late and false alarms, is maximized at
**`r sprintf("%.3f", best_u$utility_norm)`** (normalized: 0 = never alarm,
1 = per-hour oracle) at a risk threshold of `r sprintf("%.2f", best_u$threshold)`.
A positive score means the model adds value over silence on this genuinely hard,
incident-only ICU task.

The clinically decisive picture is the **alarm burden**:

```{r t4tab}
show <- al[al$threshold %in% c(op90$threshold, al$threshold[which.min(abs(al$sensitivity-0.7))], op50$threshold), ]
kable(show, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Threshold","Sensitivity","False alarms / patient-day","Frac. non-septic pts alarmed"),
      caption = "Operating points: earlier/more-sensitive detection costs rapidly rising false-alarm burden.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

```{r alarm, fig.cap="Sensitivity versus false-alarm burden for the real-time supermodel. High sensitivity is reachable only at an alarm rate that would fatigue bedside staff.", out.width="62%"}
include_graphics(fig("alarm_tradeoff.png"))
```

Catching 90% of septic patients in a timely window costs about
**`r sprintf("%.1f", op90$fa_per_patient_day)` false alarms per patient-day**,
firing on `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100*op90$frac_nonseptic_pts_alarmed)` of
non-septic patients: untenable alarm fatigue. A calmer operating point
(`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100*op50$sensitivity)` sensitivity) drops that to
`r sprintf("%.1f", op50$fa_per_patient_day)` per patient-day. This is the
number a deployment decision actually turns on.

# Tier 5: subgroup fairness (external validation deferred)

External validation on eICU is deferred (no eICU database is present locally).
Within MIMIC-IV, the Tier-1 risk is well calibrated and similarly discriminating
across sex and age bands: a model can discriminate well overall yet fail a
subgroup, which is not the case here.

```{r t5tab}
kable(sg, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Subgroup","n","Event rate","AUROC","Mean pred.","Obs. rate","Calib. ratio"),
      caption = "Subgroup discrimination and calibration-in-the-large (ratio near 1.0 = well calibrated).") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position","scale_down"))
```

# Tier 6: group-based trajectory modelling (GBTM)

The literature review's comparable MIMIC-IV statistical studies (Yang et al.
2022) use **group-based trajectory modelling** to summarise repeated SOFA
scores into a small number of latent trajectory classes, then link class
membership to mortality via Cox regression. The earlier temporal report used
a within-patient HMM instead, which clusters *states within one patient*, not
*trajectory shapes across patients*: a different technique. Tier 6 closes
that gap: a latent-class growth model (flexmix's grouped-mixture-of-regressions
formulation) is fit to first-24h SOFA trajectories on the sampled panel
(2,438 stays with sufficient repeated observations), selecting the number of
classes `r K6` by BIC.

```{r gbtm-fig, fig.cap="GBTM: latent SOFA-trajectory classes over the first 24 ICU hours.", out.width="62%"}
include_graphics(fig("gbtm_trajectories.png"))
```

Class membership shows a strong, monotonic dose-response relationship with
both outcomes, exactly as Yang et al.'s design intends:

```{r t6cox}
kable(gc, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Term","Hazard ratio","p-value"),
      caption = "Cox model: in-hospital mortality by GBTM trajectory class (reference = mildest class), adjusted for age.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

```{r t6onset}
kable(go, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Term","Odds ratio","p-value"),
      caption = "Logistic model: incident Sepsis-3 by GBTM trajectory class (reference = mildest class); this project's own outcome of interest, beyond Yang et al.'s mortality-only design.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

The steeply-worsening trajectory class carries several-fold higher mortality
and Sepsis-3 risk than the mild, flat class: the SOFA trajectory *shape*,
not just its hour-24 endpoint, is informative, consistent with the
project's broader finding that dynamics carry signal a snapshot misses.

# Tier 7: confounder-adjusted causal analysis

Every prior tier reports an *association* (a risk score, a hazard ratio). The
literature review's causal-adjustment studies (Guo et al. 2025; Zou et al.
2022) go further, using **propensity score matching (PSM)**, **inverse
probability weighting (IPW)**, and **doubly robust estimation** to estimate a
confounder-adjusted treatment effect: a method family absent from this
pipeline until now. Tier 7 asks: does administering antibiotics within 3h of
ICU admission (the Surviving Sepsis Campaign's "hour-3 bundle" threshold)
causally lower in-hospital mortality among Sepsis-3 patients, once baseline
severity and case-mix confounding is adjusted for? Confounding by indication
is the concern here: sicker patients may be treated faster, or slower if
sepsis isn't yet recognised, so a naive comparison is biased in an unknown
direction.

Following Guo et al.'s design, the adjustment set is chosen by **LASSO**
(not by hand) from age, sex, admission type, ICU type, race, and the six
SOFA organ components; all 11 candidates survived penalization. Four
estimators of increasing robustness are compared:

```{r t7tab}
kable(ce, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Method","Estimand","Risk diff.","RD 95% CI low","RD 95% CI high",
                    "Odds ratio","OR 95% CI low","OR 95% CI high"),
      caption = "Effect of early (<=3h) vs delayed antibiotics on in-hospital mortality, Sepsis-3 cohort.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position","scale_down"))
```

```{r t7fig, fig.cap="Covariate balance (standardized mean difference) before and after propensity-score matching.", out.width="70%"}
include_graphics(fig("tier7_balance_love_plot.png"))
```

Matching brings every covariate's standardized mean difference below the
conventional 0.1 threshold (figure above). All four estimators (crude,
PSM, IPW, and the doubly robust augmented-IPW estimator, consistent if
*either* the propensity model *or* the outcome model is correctly specified)
agree in direction and magnitude: early antibiotics associate with lower
mortality (PSM OR `r sprintf("%.3f", psm_row$odds_ratio)`, 95% CI
`r sprintf("%.3f", psm_row$or_ci_low)`-`r sprintf("%.3f", psm_row$or_ci_high)`;
IPW OR `r sprintf("%.3f", ipw_row$odds_ratio)`, 95% CI
`r sprintf("%.3f", ipw_row$or_ci_low)`-`r sprintf("%.3f", ipw_row$or_ci_high)`;
doubly robust risk difference `r sprintf("%.3f", aipw_row$risk_difference)`,
95% CI `r sprintf("%.3f", aipw_row$rd_ci_low)` to
`r sprintf("%.3f", aipw_row$rd_ci_high)`). Agreement across four estimators
built on different assumptions is the strongest evidence this pipeline offers
for the finding being a real association rather than residual confounding,
though, as an observational analysis, it cannot rule out unmeasured
confounders (e.g. severity-of-illness trends not captured by day-1 SOFA).

# Conclusion

This report reaches the project's real-time goal without leaving classical
statistics. A **full-feature nomogram** sets the honest ceiling
(AUROC `r sprintf("%.3f", en_auc)`) and shows informative measurement patterns
dominate the signal; a **dynamic landmark supermodel** delivers a single,
interpretable, hourly-updating risk that matches per-landmark models across the
stay; **GEE and time-varying Cox** handle the within-patient correlation the
earlier analysis ignored (within-patient correlation `r sprintf("%.2f", alpha)`,
cluster-robust SEs up to `r sprintf("%.1fx", se_infl_max)` the naive ones); a
**utility- and alarm-based evaluation** exposes the real cost of a sensitive
alarm; **GBTM** shows the shape of a patient's SOFA trajectory, not just its
level, predicts both mortality and incident sepsis; and a **PSM/IPW/doubly
robust** causal analysis finds a consistent, confounder-adjusted mortality
benefit for early antibiotics across four estimators. The remaining honest
gap is external validation, which awaits a second database (eICU). Nothing
here required a neural network; the discrimination ceiling is set by the
label's dependence on clinician recognition, not by model class.
